title: The Gang Gets Invincible

jokes.text: Opening argument: a mouse vs. scorpion debate, with Frank insisting a rat could kill a scorpion but a mouse couldn't
jokes.setup: The gang is apparently mid-heated argument about which animal would win in a fight
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies 'No shit, Frank, but we're not talking about a rat' — the entire premise is revealed to be a pointless, passionate debate about nothing
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold open — we drop in on a passionate argument about something completely idiotic. The specificity (mouse vs. scorpion vs. rat) and Frank's pedantic correction that escalates rather than resolves the argument is well-characterized. Works because it immediately establishes the gang's dynamic without setup.

jokes.text: The gang goes outside for 'fresh air' and immediately wants to go back inside: 'It's goddamn bright out here. It's so bright. I can't use my eyes.'
jokes.setup: Mac gives an inspiring speech about fresh air, blue sky, earth beneath their feet — everyone agrees it's great
jokes.punchline: Within seconds of being outside they're all miserable: too bright, people playing football near them, no room to drink
jokes.explanation: Structurally very tight — the buildup of Mac's inspirational speech with everyone earnestly agreeing ('Yeah, some uh, earth beneath our feet') followed by the near-instant reversal is perfectly executed. 'I can't use my eyes' as the specific complaint about sunlight is a great character-specific line. The gap between aspiration and reality is closed within about 30 seconds of screen time, which is excellent economy. The specificity of 'there are people playing football right next to us, like there's no room to drink' as a grievance is pitch-perfect for these characters.

jokes.text: 'There's people playing football right next to us. Like there's no room to drink.'
jokes.setup: They're annoyed about being outside
jokes.punchline: The complaint is specifically that football players are impeding their drinking — 'no room to drink' as if that's the natural outdoor activity
jokes.explanation: Good economy — 'no room to drink' reframes the outdoors as primarily a drinking venue. Solid but secondary to the bigger joke around it.

jokes.text: Dennis recognizing the movie Invincible: 'Oh! Was that the one where the guy from the New Kids on the Block makes it onto the Eagles?'
jokes.setup: Guy at the park mentions the Eagles tryouts are like the movie Invincible
jokes.punchline: Dennis confidently misidentifies the star of Invincible as a New Kids on the Block member (it's Mark Wahlberg)
jokes.explanation: Solid joke — Mark Wahlberg was famously in New Kids on the Block, so this is an almost-right cultural reference delivered with total confidence. It's the kind of thing where Dennis is simultaneously wrong and sort of not wrong, which is funnier than being completely wrong. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Mac tells Dee 'You're a woman' — then the gang lists women's sports as 'cooking,' 'complaining to your friends about your boyfriends,' 'playing at ballet,' 'cleaning,' 'displaying cars at auto shows in tiny bikinis,' and 'playing bridge when you get older'
jokes.setup: Dee reasonably argues she should be allowed to try out
jokes.punchline: The gang's list of 'women's sports' escalates from vaguely defensible to increasingly absurd and specific, ending with 'displaying cars at auto shows in tiny bikinis'
jokes.explanation: The escalating list structure works extremely well — each addition is worse than the last, and the specificity of 'displaying cars at auto shows in tiny bikinis' and 'playing bridge when you get older' shows genuine comedic craft. The show is critiquing sexism through the awfulness of its characters, which is Always Sunny's signature move. Each addition to the list gets more ludicrous, which is proper escalation structure.

jokes.text: Mac tells Dee she can't try out: 'You... You're a woman. Women can't do things like this. You'll get hurt.'
jokes.setup: Dee wants to join the tryout competition
jokes.punchline: Mac's objection isn't the logical 'women aren't allowed in NFL tryouts' — his first instinct is patronizing sexism delivered as obvious fact
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac character beat — his instinct is reflexive chauvinism before logic. Works because it's consistent with who he is.

jokes.text: The gang lists 'sports women can try out for': 'Like, uh, cooking and... Complaining to your friends about your boyfriends... Playing at ballet... Cleaning. Displaying cars at auto shows in tiny bikinis... When you get older, you can play bridge together.'
jokes.setup: Mac says there are 'plenty of other sports women can try out for'
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from vaguely plausible (ballet) to absurdly non-sport (complaining to friends about boyfriends, cleaning, auto show bikini displays, bridge)
jokes.explanation: This is a great escalating list joke. It starts somewhat grounded (cooking, ballet) and devolves into 'displaying cars at auto shows in tiny bikinis' which is both very specific and completely disconnected from sports. The characters are enthusiastically building on each other's terrible answers, which makes it funnier than if one person had said it all. 'Complaining to your friends about your boyfriends' as a sport is particularly absurd. High quotability.

jokes.text: Mac's concern isn't about fairness — it's about personal embarrassment: 'You think that's even a possibility? 'Cause that could be very embarrassing for us.'
jokes.setup: Dee argues she's in better shape than them and could outrun them
jokes.punchline: Mac's real objection to Dee competing is revealed: not principle, but fear that she might actually beat them
jokes.explanation: Good character reveal. Mac's sexism is not principled — it's self-protective. The irony is rich and character-specific.

jokes.text: Mac desperately checks whether Dee is actually allowed to try out: 'You can't try out! You're not allowed to try out. That is a rule, right? Check the rules.'
jokes.setup: Mac has confidently told Dee women can't try out for football
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he has no idea if that's actually true and panics at the possibility Dee could embarrass them
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Mac's bluster evaporating into genuine insecurity about being shown up by Dee is perfectly in-character. The rapid-fire 'that is a rule, right? Check the rules' shows authentic panic beneath the machismo.

jokes.text: Charlie setting up to tailgate the NFL tryouts with beer and a margarita machine while others try to make the team
jokes.setup: Everyone else is treating the tryout seriously
jokes.punchline: Charlie and Frank's plan is to set up a full tailgate with 'a layer of beer, then a layer of ice' and a margarita machine — not to try out, just to drink next to the tryouts
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific — the idea of Charlie and Frank treating a professional sports tryout as a drinking opportunity is entirely consistent with who they are. The margarita machine is a good specific detail. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Green Man backstory: 'In high school, Charlie was like our school mascot. A mascot nobody wanted. He'd get wasted and dress in this green spandex bodysuit.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks what Green Man is
jokes.punchline: 'A mascot nobody wanted' — the specific addition that the school actively didn't want him as mascot makes it much darker and funnier than just 'he was a mascot'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a mascot nobody wanted' is excellent — it implies rejection, sadness, and Charlie's complete obliviousness to social cues all at once. The addition of 'he'd get wasted' is perfectly Charlie. Good economy in delivering a lot of character pathos in one line.

jokes.text: Charlie defending Green Man: 'Green Man was good. It got me through some hard times. But I'm done with it.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are ribbing Charlie about the Green Man suit
jokes.punchline: Charlie's earnest, sincere defense of a green spandex bodysuit as an emotional support mechanism — 'got me through some hard times' — delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: The sadness underneath the joke is what makes it work. Charlie genuinely means it — the spandex suit helped him cope with something — and his sincerity makes it simultaneously funny and oddly touching. 'But I'm done with it' as the final note of closure on a green bodysuit is perfectly Charlie. High character integration score because only Charlie could make this line land.

jokes.text: Mac's Woodstock reference: Dennis asks if Mac is planning on 'getting himself locked in the bathroom of his cousin's Winnebago for three days'
jokes.setup: Mac says this is gonna be exactly like Woodstock
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals Mac's specific Woodstock experience was being trapped in a Winnebago bathroom for three days
jokes.explanation: Great comedic revelation — the specificity of 'cousin's Winnebago' is perfect, and the fact that Mac's fondest festival memory involves being trapped in a bathroom for three days is both darkly funny and entirely believable for this character. The setup of claiming it'll be 'like Woodstock' primes for romance/nostalgia, the punchline deflates it completely.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I survived on hand soap and toilet water for three days. The memory haunts me.'
jokes.setup: Mac was defending his Woodstock memory
jokes.punchline: 'The memory haunts me' — delivered as a sincere traumatic confession about hand soap and toilet water, treating it with the gravity of a war story
jokes.explanation: The final beat of this story is the best part — 'The memory haunts me' is delivered with absolute solemnity about surviving on bathroom soap. The economy here is exceptional: four words do enormous work, treating a grotesque mundane experience as genuine trauma. Highly quotable precisely because it takes something silly with total seriousness. This is the kind of line that gets repeated.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis excited to look down at the yard markers to 'literally see how many yards I'm running' — then noticing 15 guys wearing capes
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis arrive at the Linc hyped up about the tryouts
jokes.punchline: 15 guys wearing capes at a football tryout, and Dennis's earnest indignation: 'What advantage does that give you? Absolutely none.'
jokes.explanation: The image of 15 guys in capes at a football tryout is funny on its own. Dennis analyzing capes from a performance standpoint ('what advantage does that give you?') is a great character beat — his self-seriousness applied to something absurd. Solid visual comedy moment.

jokes.text: 15 people wearing capes to the tryout: 'I've seen a lot of people wearing capes. There are, like, 15 guys wearing capes. Why would you wear a cape? What advantage does that give you? Absolutely none.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are excited to arrive at the tryout
jokes.punchline: The tryout is full of delusional people wearing superhero capes, which Mac analyzes purely from a tactical football standpoint
jokes.explanation: Funny visual world-building. Mac's earnest tactical analysis of why a cape gives no football advantage is funnier than simply pointing out capes are weird. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Frank can't urinate because Dennis is standing next to him talking to him: 'You're standing next to me, you're talking to me. It's making me nervous, and I can't do my thing.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if Frank is done urinating
jokes.punchline: Frank explains the social pressure of someone watching him pee has prevented him from starting at all — then immediately asks for another beer
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny urination anxiety bit. The request for another beer immediately after is a good Frank touch. Functional but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Frank casually offers to drop acid: 'Want to drop some acid with me?' / Charlie: 'Well, no. Thank you. I believe that would have the complete opposite effect of relaxation for me.'
jokes.setup: Frank is set up to 'relax' at the tailgate
jokes.punchline: Frank's relaxation plan involves LSD. Charlie's overly formal refusal — 'I believe that would have the complete opposite effect of relaxation for me' — treats drug use as a polite social offer to decline
jokes.explanation: Two good jokes in one exchange: Frank treating acid as a casual relaxation tool, and Charlie's weirdly formal and thoughtful refusal of it. 'I believe that would have the complete opposite effect of relaxation for me' is funny because it's such a measured, reasonable response to a highly unreasonable offer. Charlie's self-awareness here is a nice character contrast.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Well, I'm gonna trip balls.'
jokes.setup: Charlie declines the acid
jokes.punchline: Frank's completely matter-of-fact declaration that he will be taking acid regardless, stated as casually as announcing he'll have a sandwich
jokes.explanation: Four words of perfect Frank energy. The casual finality of it — no justification, no buildup — is the whole joke. The economy is nearly perfect. This is a highly quotable Frank line precisely because it's so short and so him.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis applying makeup to each other, arguing about cheekbones and foundation: 'That's 'cause I have good cheekbones.' / 'You have good cheekbones?' / 'Yeah. That's 'cause you put foundation all over, bro.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are applying makeup to each other, apparently arguing about technique
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims his cheekbones are good; Mac reveals Dennis put 'foundation all over' — the absurdity of two tough guys arguing about makeup technique and cheekbones
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny bit — Mac and Dennis's homoerotic tension and mutual vanity expressed through cosmetics. Dennis's pride in his cheekbones is very on-brand. The visual of them doing each other's makeup before a football tryout does heavy lifting. High character integration because this joke is entirely about who these two specific people are.

jokes.text: Dee shows up disguised as a man. Mac: 'This is a joke, right? You think anyone's gonna buy that?' / 'Whatever, bro. You're gonna get crushed.'
jokes.setup: Dee said she wanted to try out but was told women can't
jokes.punchline: Dee appears disguised as a male football player — the visual gag of her disguise clearly not being convincing
jokes.explanation: The visual of Dee in a bad disguise is a reliable comedy premise. The brothers' immediate dismissal is on-brand. Gets more of its impact from the visual than from the writing itself.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Dee, the second any part of your body touches that field, it's gonna shatter like glass. You got bones like glass.' / 'You spent half your life in a back brace. Your body's, like, 90% scoliosis, Dee.'
jokes.setup: Dee is in disguise and confident she can compete
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis systematically dismantle Dee's physical body — 'bones like glass,' 'half your life in a back brace,' '90% scoliosis' — delivered with casual cruelty
jokes.explanation: 'Bones like glass' becomes a running gag through the episode and pays off at the end. '90% scoliosis' is a great made-up statistic delivered with authority. The escalation from 'shatter like glass' to 'half your life in a back brace' to '90% scoliosis' is well-structured cruelty with good comedic rhythm.

jokes.text: The tryouts aren't at Lincoln Financial Field — they're at 'a shitty high school in Bucks County'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been dreaming about playing on the Linc — the actual Eagles stadium
jokes.punchline: The coach's withering 'You think you dipshits are gonna play on the same field that champions play on?' followed by the reveal it's a Bucks County high school
jokes.explanation: Classic deflation joke — the buildup of Mac and Dennis's excitement about the Linc makes the reveal of a Bucks County high school land harder. The coach's contemptuous 'dipshits' and 'where champions play' framing is well-structured. The specificity of 'Bucks County' as the comedically mundane alternative to the Linc is a good local joke.

jokes.text: Coach repeating 'Sprint to the bus. Sprint to the bus. Sprint to the bus.' in an increasingly exasperated way
jokes.setup: Everyone needs to get on the bus
jokes.punchline: The coach's monotone, resigned repetition of the same phrase — 'If I say it one more time... Sprint to the bus' — implies he's dealt with idiots all day
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny running bit — the coach's exasperated repetition implies a whole backstory of dealing with incompetent tryout attendees. Functional but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis miss the bus and are left at the empty Linc: 'Maybe they're having the tryouts in a different place.' / 'Son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Everyone sprinted to the bus while Mac and Dennis apparently weren't paying attention
jokes.punchline: Dennis's desperate attempt to find an innocent explanation ('maybe they're having the tryouts in a different place') immediately undercut by Mac's resigned 'Son of a bitch'
jokes.explanation: Good small beat — Dennis's optimistic denial is very him, Mac's resignation is very him. Brief but character-specific.

jokes.text: Frank doesn't want to pack up and follow the bus: 'No, this is so much work. Charlie, get up. This is work. I didn't want to...'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis tell Frank and Charlie they need to follow the bus to the actual tryout location
jokes.punchline: Frank and Charlie's extreme reluctance to pack up the tailgate they just set up — treating moving as an enormous burden
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing but relatively thin. The laziness joke is functional without being particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Doyle McPoyle's bus conversation: 'I like your mustache.' / 'Oh. Thank you. Hmm. I can't grow one.' / 'That's a pretty sweet cape. Thank you. My mom made it.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are stuck on the bus with strangers
jokes.punchline: The bizarre stilted small talk with a McPoyle — complimenting a fake mustache and a cape, then learning mom made the cape — lands as deeply uncomfortable pseudo-normal conversation
jokes.explanation: The McPoyle social register — almost-normal but slightly off — is well-rendered. 'My mom made it. She did a very good job. Yeah. She's talented.' is a genuinely uncomfortable bit of bus small talk. The staccato rhythm of the dialogue creates the awkward energy effectively.

jokes.text: Doyle McPoyle's speech: 'When I'm done with this tryout, you'll go back to your sad, pitiful life, and I'll be on the Eagles. And everybody in Philadelphia will know the name McPoyle.'
jokes.setup: Doyle gets into a trash-talking argument with Mac and Dennis on the bus
jokes.punchline: Doyle's total sincerity in believing he will be a Philadelphia Eagle and the name 'McPoyle' will be celebrated — delivered with zero self-awareness from someone who is clearly a McPoyle
jokes.explanation: The McPoyle family is one of the show's great recurring joke factories, and the idea of someone named McPoyle believing Philadelphia will celebrate that name is pitch-perfect. The grandiosity of 'everybody in Philadelphia will know the name McPoyle' plays against everything we know about the McPoyles. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis recognizing Doyle as a McPoyle from physical features: 'The unibrow. Yeah. The eczema. The acne. He's definitely a McPoyle. There are so many of those people.'
jokes.setup: Doyle reveals his last name is McPoyle
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis identify him as a McPoyle by cataloguing his physical ailments, then the casual observation 'there are so many of those people'
jokes.explanation: The running McPoyle family joke gets deepened here — the idea that there are so many McPoyles that Mac and Dennis can identify them by a checklist of ailments is a great piece of mythology-building comedy. 'There are so many of those people' is delivered with resigned familiarity that implies a long history.

jokes.text: Frank taking more acid: 'What are you doing, dude?' / 'Taking more acid.' / 'Classic mistake, Frank. You're making a classic mistake, bro.'
jokes.setup: Frank is already on acid from earlier
jokes.punchline: Frank takes more acid. Charlie's response treats this as a known category of error — 'classic mistake' — implying familiarity with this mistake being made repeatedly
jokes.explanation: 'Classic mistake, Frank' is excellent — it implies this is a recognized, documented phenomenon in Charlie's world. The tone of weary expertise from Charlie about drug overdosing mistakes is perfectly calibrated. High economy — four words do a lot of characterization work.

jokes.text: The McPoyle family tailgate — including someone with a jar of pig parts, someone apparently sensitive to sunlight ('It's gonna hurt your eyes'), and someone playing a fife
jokes.setup: Charlie and Frank discover the entire McPoyle family has shown up
jokes.punchline: The McPoyle family reveals itself in layers: the whole family is there, someone has a jar of pig parts, someone has thin corneas, someone plays a fife — each reveal more bizarre than the last
jokes.explanation: The McPoyle family reveal is a great escalating absurdist sequence. 'What is that a jar of?' / 'Pig parts.' is a fantastic exchange — the casual answer to a horrified question. 'They've got thin corneas' implies someone anticipated needing to explain this. The fife is an inspired detail — not a guitar, not a banjo, but a fife — perfectly off. Each element builds the portrait of a genuinely bizarre extended family.

jokes.text: 'How many can there possibly be?' — Charlie's reaction to the full McPoyle family arriving
jokes.setup: Charlie discovers the McPoyle numbers are vast
jokes.punchline: Charlie's existential despair at the sheer quantity of McPoyles
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat but relatively thin on its own — works better as part of the larger McPoyle reveal sequence (joke 28). The horror at McPoyle proliferation is a consistent joke in the show.

jokes.text: McPoyle family member with apparent light sensitivity: 'You're here in the world. That's the sun. It's gonna hurt your eyes. Watch your mouth. They've got thin corneas.'
jokes.setup: More McPoyles emerge from the bus
jokes.punchline: One family member apparently can't be in sunlight and needs to be introduced to the concept of the outdoors; they have 'thin corneas'
jokes.explanation: 'They've got thin corneas' as a casual medical detail about a family member is exactly the right level of specific grotesque detail. The McPoyles work because their afflictions are described matter-of-factly.

jokes.text: Charlie trying to introduce someone apparently on a very bad trip to the concept of the sun: 'You're... you're here in the world. That's the sun. It's gonna hurt your eyes.'
jokes.setup: A McPoyle appears to be very disoriented or possibly also on substances
jokes.punchline: Charlie explaining basic existence to this person — 'you're here in the world' — implies the person needs to be oriented to reality itself
jokes.explanation: 'You're here in the world. That's the sun.' is a genuinely great line — the gentle, concerned explanation of basic reality to someone who apparently needs it is both absurd and weirdly compassionate. It implies a McPoyle so out of touch with reality that the sun needs to be identified. Highly quotable non-sequitur.

jokes.text: Charlie refusing to fist-bump a McPoyle: 'I'm not bumping your fist. / Bump it. / Do it, Charlie. Bump it. / I'm not bumping you, all right? I never bumped him once! I'm not gonna bump him!'
jokes.setup: A McPoyle offers a fist bump as a gesture of goodwill
jokes.punchline: Charlie's total refusal to fist bump the McPoyle, delivered with escalating passion — 'I never bumped him once!' implies a long history of refusing this specific request
jokes.explanation: 'I never bumped him once!' is a great line — it implies Charlie has been asked to fist-bump this McPoyle multiple times across their history and has refused every single time. The passion of the refusal about something so trivial is very Charlie. Good character integration and history-building.

jokes.text: Cole Armstrong's introduction: 'Cole. Cole Armstrong. Three-time all-American. Fastest sprinter in five counties.' Then immediately asking the coach 'Would you like us to stand when you address us, or do you prefer we take a knee?' Coach: 'I don't give a shit!'
jokes.setup: An overly serious tryout participant introduces himself with excessive credentials
jokes.punchline: Cole's attempt at military-style protocol ('take a knee') is dismissed entirely by the coach's 'I don't give a shit' — immediately deflating Cole's entire self-presentation
jokes.explanation: Cole Armstrong works as a one-episode character because his earnestness about these tryouts is completely misplaced. The 'five counties' credential for a public Eagles tryout is a great absurd detail. The military protocol question being shot down with 'I don't give a shit' is a satisfying deflation.

jokes.text: Coach explaining why tryouts exist: 'We're doing these tryouts for you, because of your harassment and your love for the New Kids on the Block movie. You paid your $30 fee.'
jokes.setup: The coach addresses the crowd of tryout hopefuls
jokes.punchline: The tryouts exist because fans harassed the Eagles enough and paid $30 each — stripping all romance from the premise
jokes.explanation: Great cynical take — the Eagles are doing this purely because they were harassed and took people's money, not because of any inspirational belief in the public. The deflation of the Invincible/American dream premise is sharp and very Sunny in its worldview. '$30 fee' as the price of a dream is a perfect detail.

jokes.text: Donovan McNabb's motivational speech turns out to be a McDonald's advertisement: 'I'm here to tell you that you can, too, if you start every day with a hearty breakfast from McDonald's. Like the new Sausage Egg McGriddle Value Meal, available now for a limited time for under five dollars. Remember, guys. Real champs eat at McDonald's. I'm lovin' it. Can I get the check?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are hyped to see Donovan McNabb give them a motivational speech
jokes.punchline: The 'keynote speaker' gives a pure McDonald's commercial, ending with 'Can I get the check?' — the mercenary reality of celebrity appearances stripped bare
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: massive buildup of McNabb anticipation, the speech begins inspirationally ('I'm here to tell you that you can, too'), then pivots immediately into an ad read with specific product details (Sausage Egg McGriddle, under five dollars, limited time). The final 'Can I get the check?' is the killer — he's not even pretending it was anything other than a paid appearance. The joke skewers celebrity endorsement culture, the false promise of inspirational events, and the Eagles organization's cynical use of the tryouts simultaneously. Comparable to an 8-9 anchor for its satirical precision and the comedic structure.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis debating whether McNabb is actually the guy from The Cosby Show: 'Was that the guy from The Cosby Show? He was married to Sondra. Alvin. Alvin. They had Raven-Symoné. That's So Raven.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting to the fake McNabb commercial
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis go down a confident rabbit hole of wrong pop culture connections — Cosby Show, Sondra, Alvin, Raven-Symoné — with each step being slightly off but delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: The cascading wrong pop culture reference chain is a great Mac and Dennis bit — each person builds on the other's wrong information with equal confidence. 'That's So Raven' as the final landing point of this chain is an inspired absurdist endpoint. The comedy is in the total conviction with which they pursue this clearly wrong tangent.

jokes.text: Frank on acid reporting symptoms: 'I'm starting to feel it. / I bet you are, bud. / Feeling weird. / Yeah. You're probably feeling very weird. / The acid's making me feel like I gotta take a dump.'
jokes.setup: Frank is beginning to feel the effects of the acid
jokes.punchline: Frank's acid trip symptoms culminate in needing to take a dump — the most mundane possible psychedelic complaint
jokes.explanation: The deflation of psychedelic experience into 'I gotta take a dump' is funny — Frank's acid trip is about as unglamorous as possible. Charlie's patient, matter-of-fact responses 'I bet you are, bud' and 'Yeah. You're probably feeling very weird' imply he's done this before. Good character work.

jokes.text: Frank reveals he secretly dosed Charlie's beer: 'I put a shitload of it in your beer.' / Charlie: 'What? Yeah. Is that what all those little pieces of paper were floating... I drank all that shit, dude!'
jokes.setup: Charlie asks if anything has kicked in yet, thinking he means beer
jokes.punchline: Frank reveals he secretly put 'a shitload of acid' in Charlie's beer because he 'didn't want to be the only one tripping' — Charlie realizes the paper pieces he drank were the acid
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best revelations. Frank dosing Charlie without consent because 'I don't want to be the only one tripping' is perfectly Frank — completely selfish, matter-of-fact about the transgression. 'Is that what all those little pieces of paper were floating...' shows Charlie's dawning horror. The 'why would you do that?' / 'I don't want to be the only one tripping' exchange is a perfect Frank justification — self-evident to him, completely monstrous to everyone else. High character integration.

jokes.text: Frank secretly dosed Charlie's beer: 'I put a shitload of it in your beer.' / 'Is that what all those little pieces of paper were floating...' / 'I drank all that shit, dude!'
jokes.setup: Charlie declines acid; Frank asks how he's feeling
jokes.punchline: Frank secretly dosed Charlie with 'a shitload' of acid; Charlie realizes he consumed all of it, which explains the floating paper
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup and payoff. The misdirection is clean — Charlie declined, so we don't expect him to be dosed. Frank's reasoning ('I don't want to be the only one tripping') is perfectly Frank Reynolds: selfish, completely logical within his own moral framework. Charlie's realization ('Is that what all those little pieces of paper were...') is a great comedic beat — he consumed the evidence unknowingly. High craft, high impact.

jokes.text: Cole Armstrong taunting Mac and Dennis after sprints: 'You ready to quit yet, Cole? Yeah. We ran for, like, 10 minutes. My side is gonna explode.'
jokes.setup: Cole has been mocking Mac and Dennis throughout
jokes.punchline: Cole's trash talk about Mac and Dennis quitting, while Mac's internal monologue reveals they ran for 'like 10 minutes' and his side is going to explode
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the contrast between Cole's trash talk and Mac and Dennis's actual physical state (10 minutes of sprinting nearly killing them) is effective. Dennis being 'in so much pain' after a brief run against his self-image as an athlete is consistent character comedy.

jokes.text: Dennis picks Cole as his hitting drill partner: 'I pick Cole!' — Cole launches himself at Dennis and apparently destroys him
jokes.setup: Dennis confidently selects the most athletic person at the tryout as his hitting partner
jokes.punchline: Dennis's confidence in picking Cole is immediately shown to be catastrophically wrong as Cole apparently levels him
jokes.explanation: The setup works because Dennis's confidence is so total and so misplaced. The aftermath — 'Oh, no, he didn't! That's my dance. That's my signature dance' from Mac watching Cole celebrate — implies Dennis got absolutely crushed. Visual slapstick that relies on implication but lands well.

jokes.text: Frank avoiding hitting drills: 'Ah. Uh, hitting's not really my thing, Coach.' Coach: 'Spoken like a true champion. You just might make the team.' Frank: 'Awesome. Really?'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to avoid doing hitting drills
jokes.punchline: The coach's withering sarcasm ('spoken like a true champion') goes entirely over Frank's head — he takes it literally and is thrilled
jokes.explanation: One of the best small exchanges in the episode. The structure is tight: Frank's cowardly deflection, the coach's sarcastic non-sequitur, then Frank's completely genuine 'Awesome. Really?' — he has no idea he's being mocked. Frank's obliviousness and his genuine excitement at potentially making the Eagles is perfect character work. The economy is excellent — three short lines and three distinct comic beats. 'Jesus Christ' from someone offscreen is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Dennis's hitting drill: 'Eeny, meeny, miny, mo' — picks Frank, who is the most incompetent person there
jokes.setup: Dennis needs to pick a hitting partner
jokes.punchline: He uses 'eeny meeny miny mo' — a child's selection method — and lands on Frank, the worst possible partner for a football drill
jokes.explanation: Decent bit. 'Eeny meeny miny mo' as Dennis's selection strategy at an NFL tryout is the right level of pathetic, but it's not especially inventive.

jokes.text: Frank talks to himself trying to exit the porta-potty while on acid: 'Okay, Frank. That was easy. Now just exit. Don't talk to anybody. These people are freak shows. Wait. Wait. Better wash your hands. No telling what kind of germs these McPoyles have.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to navigate the world while on a heavy acid trip
jokes.punchline: Frank gives himself a multi-step pep talk to exit a porta-potty, including remembering to wash his hands (paranoid about McPoyle germs), then getting trapped again
jokes.explanation: Frank's self-coaching on a dose of acid is well-rendered — the specificity of 'no telling what kind of germs these McPoyles have' is funny because his paranoid acid logic lands on actual McPoyle-specific concern. The fact that he immediately gets trapped again anyway makes the whole self-coaching exercise pointless.

jokes.text: Frank getting locked in the porta-potty again: 'Oh! Crap! / What the hell? Oh, no. Not again. / Oh, no! Hey! Hey! Hey! Somebody get me outta here!'
jokes.setup: Frank tried to exit carefully and wash his hands
jokes.punchline: Despite all his careful self-coaching, Frank immediately gets trapped in the porta-potty again
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Frank trapped in the portable toilet pays off adequately — 'Not again' implies this has happened before. Functions well as a payoff to the previous self-coaching bit but isn't particularly inventive on its own.

jokes.text: McPoyle brother discussing Doyle's diet: 'It's probably 'cause he eats all that fish.' / Dennis: 'What is going on with his head? It's too small or tight or something.' / McPoyle: 'Yeah, that's it. His skin's too tight.' / 'My skin's not tight.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are stuck next to McPoyle brothers who are narrating Doyle's performance
jokes.punchline: The conversation about Doyle's physical attributes — 'his head's too small or tight,' 'his skin's too tight,' 'my skin's not tight' — is surreal and uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: 'His skin's too tight' is a great McPoyle-specific absurd physical description. The fact that Doyle defends himself — 'my skin's not tight' — with apparent sincerity, treating this as a credible accusation to be rebutted, makes it very funny. The fish diet explanation delivered with complete confidence adds to the McPoyle mythology.

jokes.text: Dennis's internal monologue while running routes: 'My form is perfect. I'm like Jerry Rice. Feel that stride. So fluid and fast. I've got the stride of a gazelle. A beautiful, beautiful gazelle person.'
jokes.setup: Dennis runs out for a pass
jokes.punchline: Dennis's narcissistic internal monologue ('I'm like Jerry Rice,' 'the stride of a gazelle') plays against whatever we're meant to understand his actual performance looks like
jokes.explanation: 'A beautiful, beautiful gazelle person' is the standout line — the specific self-compliment, the repetition of 'beautiful,' and the odd addition of 'person' (as opposed to just 'gazelle') makes it perfectly Dennis. This internal monologue is one of the best character-specific jokes in the episode because it perfectly captures Dennis's pathological narcissism and self-delusion. 'I should've popped my shirt off' and wondering if women are watching from the sidelines are perfect buttons. Very high character integration — this could only be Dennis.

jokes.text: Dennis's internal thought: 'Hmm, I should've popped my shirt off. Goddamn it. Really should've popped that shirt off. I wonder if any women are watching from the sidelines.'
jokes.setup: Dennis's internal athletic monologue
jokes.punchline: His athletic fantasy pivots immediately from physical performance to sexual vanity — the shirt-off regret mid-football route reveals his actual priorities
jokes.explanation: 'Goddamn it. Really should've popped that shirt off' as a mid-route athletic regret is superb Dennis characterization. The pivot from sports performance to shirt removal to wondering if women are watching is a perfect arc of Dennis's self-obsession. This continuation of the internal monologue builds on the previous joke to create a complete portrait of Dennis's psyche.

jokes.text: Dee turns out to be an excellent kicker — the coaches are amazed: 'Holy shit! The other coaches gotta hear about this.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been certain Dee will embarrass herself and them
jokes.punchline: Dee is apparently a genuinely excellent kicker — completely subverting the expected outcome
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — the entire episode has been Mac and Dennis dismissing Dee, so her turning out to be legitimately good is a satisfying subversion. Sets up the later payoff of her breaking her foot.

jokes.text: Mac's analysis of Dee's kicking ability: 'No. Those stork-like legs... They act like pendulums. And on the bottoms of those pendulums, feet like wrecking balls.'
jokes.setup: Mac reluctantly acknowledges Dee might have been a lucky kick
jokes.punchline: Mac's scientific breakdown of Dee's anatomy as a kicking machine — pendulum legs, wrecking ball feet — delivered with impressed-but-horrified specificity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Those stork-like legs... they act like pendulums. And on the bottoms of those pendulums, feet like wrecking balls.' is a beautifully structured insult-compliment — it acknowledges Dee's ability while framing her entire body as a grotesque mechanical apparatus. The pendulum-to-wrecking-ball image is specific, visual, and perfectly terrible. It's the kind of line that makes the whole episode worth watching. High originality, perfect structure, maximum economy, and extremely character-specific (Mac would absolutely analyze Dee's body this way). Comparably excellent to the 8.0 anchor and arguably surpasses it in quotability.

jokes.text: Artemis's voice from inside the porta-potty offering to help Frank escape: 'I'm trapped. I know. But I can help. Crawl into my mouth.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trapped in the porta-potty on acid
jokes.punchline: Artemis appears and suggests Frank escape by crawling into her mouth — a surreal acid-trip solution delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: 'Crawl into my mouth.' is delivered with total sincerity and is one of the most unexpected lines in the episode. The setup of Frank being trapped is relatively simple, but Artemis's solution — not 'I'll help you out' or 'break the door' but 'crawl into my mouth' — is a genuinely bizarre and original comedic choice. Frank's response 'I don't think I can fit' treats it as a logistical problem rather than an insane suggestion, which makes it funnier. The subsequent 'sure you will, just go one leg at a time' escalates beautifully. Exceptional economy and originality.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Okay. Into the toilet I go.' — apparently climbing into the toilet to escape
jokes.setup: Artemis suggests Frank go 'one leg at a time' to crawl through her 'mouth' — which Frank apparently interprets as the toilet
jokes.punchline: Frank's matter-of-fact acceptance — 'Into the toilet I go' — before apparently climbing into a porta-potty toilet
jokes.explanation: 'Into the toilet I go.' Five words. Frank's complete serenity and acceptance about climbing into a porta-potty toilet is perfectly Frank — no protest, no revision, just 'okay, into the toilet I go.' The economy here is nearly perfect. This line has become one of the show's most quoted moments precisely because it's so short, so dark, and delivered with such misplaced dignity. Comparable to the 'I'm gonna trip balls' economy but applied to something far more extreme.

jokes.text: Charlie in the Green Man suit dancing with the entire McPoyle family while on acid: 'Man, this is crazy. You are dancing with the entire McPoyle family. These people are freak shows, man. Freaks.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is on acid in the Green Man suit at the tailgate
jokes.punchline: Charlie's internal narrative acknowledging the insanity of his situation while continuing to dance — 'you are dancing with the entire McPoyle family' — with the visual of a green spandex man dancing with the McPoyles
jokes.explanation: The visual of Green Man tripping acid and dancing with the McPoyles is a great convergence of the episode's subplots. 'You are dancing with the entire McPoyle family' as a first-person observation about one's own situation while continuing to dance is funny self-aware absurdism. This is Also a payoff to both the Green Man setup (he said he was done with it) and the McPoyle family arrival.

jokes.text: Charlie reasoning his way through the Green Man suit: 'You know why? Because you are the Green Man. Green Man is saving your life right now, bro. Just go with the flow.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is on acid, dancing with McPoyles, and trying to stay calm
jokes.punchline: Charlie's coping mechanism is the Green Man suit — the alter ego of the green spandex bodysuit is apparently an emotionally stabilizing force, validating his earlier claim that it 'got him through hard times'
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the earlier 'Green Man got me through some hard times' joke. Charlie said it sincerely and was mocked for it — now it's proven true: the Green Man suit IS helping him cope with an acid trip and McPoyle dancing. 'Green Man is saving your life right now, bro' is a beautiful piece of absurdist character-specific logic. High character integration because this whole arc is very specifically Charlie.

jokes.text: Frank is spotted trying to climb through a trash can for 20 minutes: 'He's been trying to climb through that trash can for 20 minutes. I'm pretty sure he's on acid.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are looking for Frank urgently
jokes.punchline: Frank — still tripping — has been attempting to enter a trash can for 20 minutes; Charlie reports this casually
jokes.explanation: Frank's progression from bathroom to trash can is a great escalation. 'He's been trying to climb through that trash can for 20 minutes' — the specificity of '20 minutes' makes it funnier. Charlie's matter-of-fact 'I'm pretty sure he's on acid' is delivered as new information even though he watched Frank take it.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's plan to sabotage Dee: Frank fires a gun near Dee when she punts to startle her
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are threatened by Dee outperforming them
jokes.punchline: Their solution to Dee succeeding at the tryout is to have Frank fire a gun near her — an absurd escalation of a petty rivalry into firearms
jokes.explanation: The casual escalation to firearm sabotage of a sister's football tryout is perfectly on-brand for Always Sunny — these characters are terrible people and the show commits to it. 'I'll fire the gun. It'll startle her. She'll blow the kick. That's a great plan.' delivered as a totally reasonable scheme is good dark comedy.

jokes.text: Frank on acid, confused in the Green Man suit: 'Wait, wait, wait! When the hell did I put Green Man on?' / 'That lizard talks! Where? Where? I don't like lizards! / 'Lizard, am I standing in poop?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are trying to get the gun from Frank while he's heavily tripping
jokes.punchline: Frank doesn't remember putting on the Green Man suit, is terrified of a lizard only he can see, and asks the lizard if he's standing in poop
jokes.explanation: 'Lizard, am I standing in poop?' is a highlight of the episode — it has everything: the acid hallucination, the poop anxiety (callbacks to his porta-potty experience), and addressing a hallucination formally as 'lizard.' Asking a lizard for factual information about one's physical situation is exactly the right kind of absurdist specificity. 'I don't like lizards' as a terror response is very Frank.

jokes.text: Dee's big speech about women in sports, before apparently kicking badly and breaking her foot: 'I'm about to demonstrate to all of you my natural abilities as a punter... and I'm gonna do it... as a woman.'
jokes.setup: Dee has been invited to show her kicking ability after impressing the coaches
jokes.punchline: Dee's triumphant feminist speech is set up for a spectacular failure
jokes.explanation: The speech works as an escalating setup for the disaster that follows. The sincerity of 'as a woman' — Dee revealing her disguise for maximum effect — is a good dramatic beat made funny by what it sets up. The character works here because Dee's genuine competence and her genuine fragility (literally fragile bones) are both true simultaneously.

jokes.text: Dee breaks her foot on the punt: 'Oh! Oh, I broke it. Oh, it may be broken. Oh, sweet Jesus, I think I broke it.'
jokes.setup: Dee's triumphant feminist speech and big kick
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately breaks her foot — vindicating Mac's 'bones like glass' prediction
jokes.explanation: The payoff to 'bones like glass' — Dee breaking her foot on a single punt after her triumphant speech — is well-earned. The structure is excellent: predict fragility (06:08), establish competence (16:25), set up triumph (19:27), deliver catastrophic failure (19:52). The extended 'Oh! Oh, I broke it. Oh, it may be broken. Oh, sweet Jesus, I think I broke it' is funny in its escalating self-correction.

jokes.text: Mac: 'So your bones are made out of glass.' / Dee: 'Yes! / No, my bones aren't... You know what? It doesn't matter, because I made the furthest, so I win.'
jokes.setup: Dee just broke her foot
jokes.punchline: Mac's triumphant 'so your bones are made out of glass' callback is accepted — Dee momentarily concedes then walks it back, still claiming victory despite a broken foot
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'bones like glass' landing after Dee actually breaks her foot is satisfying. Dee's refusal to concede even with a broken foot — 'I made the furthest, so I win' — is perfectly in character. The 'Yes! / No, my bones aren't' self-correction is a funny beat.

jokes.text: Nobody minds if Charlie dances: 'Nobody minds if I do a little dancing now, do they?'
jokes.setup: Crisis is unfolding with the gun and Dee's injury
jokes.punchline: Charlie, still tripping in Green Man, politely asks if anyone minds him dancing — during an emergency
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed comic beat in the middle of chaos. Charlie's polite check-in about dancing during an emergency — 'Nobody minds if I do a little dancing now, do they?' — is very funny. Good economy and character-specific (only the tripping Charlie in Green Man would think this is the right moment to ask).

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis celebrating while Dee needs medical attention: 'No, I win because you're the girl, and you got knocked unconscious. You didn't win. You got crushed. Once again!'
jokes.setup: Dee is on the ground with a broken foot claiming she won the competition
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis's victory celebration over their injured sister, treating her broken foot as a win for them
jokes.explanation: The gang's complete lack of concern for Dee's injury, treating her broken foot as their victory, is on-brand for the show's dark character comedy. 'Once again!' implies this is a recurring pattern of Dee being hurt and them being happy about it.

jokes.text: Frank accidentally shoots Doyle McPoyle in the leg: 'Holy shit. This thing is loaded.' / 'My leg! Somebody shot my leg!'
jokes.setup: Frank has the gun and is dancing, while Mac and Dennis try to get it from him
jokes.punchline: Frank accidentally shoots Doyle McPoyle in the leg — the accidental discharge of a weapon used for a petty prank plan results in actual harm
jokes.explanation: 'Holy shit. This thing is loaded.' is a perfect Frank line — his surprise that the loaded gun he's been waving around is loaded. The plan to use the gun to startle Dee escalating to actually shooting a McPoyle is excellent dark escalation that Always Sunny executes well. The specificity of Doyle getting shot (the character who was most earnestly going to 'make the Eagles') gives it extra dark irony.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's reaction to shooting a McPoyle: 'Oh, that's not good. That's not good. No. That could come back and bite us in the ass. That's not a good thing.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just accidentally shot Doyle McPoyle in the leg
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis's concern about the accidental shooting is entirely self-centered — 'could come back and bite us in the ass' — zero concern for the wounded person
jokes.explanation: Perfect Always Sunny ending beat — someone has been shot and Mac and Dennis's only thought is how it affects them. 'Could come back and bite us in the ass' as the primary concern after a shooting is a great darkly comic character beat. The repetition of 'that's not good' as an understatement for 'we just shot someone' is excellent. Very high character integration — this response is exactly who these people are.

jokes.text: Episode ends with everyone apparently fleeing the scene: 'Ready? Let's go!' — cutting away from a McPoyle bleeding on the ground
jokes.setup: Frank has just shot Doyle McPoyle
jokes.punchline: The gang simply leaves — no accountability, no help for the injured person, just 'Ready? Let's go!'
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke is the gang's total moral bankruptcy expressed in two words: 'Let's go.' The economy is nearly perfect — no explanation, no hesitation, they just run. It's the logical endpoint of the whole episode's character work and the show's ethos: these people cause harm and face zero consequences. 'Ready? Let's go!' as a closing line after accidentally shooting someone captures the show's dark soul efficiently.

tmdb_overview: Mac, Dennis and Dee try out for the Philadelphia Eagles.  Also interested in becoming an Eagle is Liam and Ryan McPoyle's brother, Doyle.
